name: Duration Estimates
purpose: Records how long each piece of project work will take to complete. An estimate can be made for each activity, work package or control account, using expert judgment or a quantitative method (parametric, analogous or three-point estimating). Where the duration is driven by people, the effort hours are converted into days or weeks.

elements.guidance: A description of the work that needs to be done.
The amount of labor needed to do the work; usually in hours, possibly in days.
The length of time needed to do the work; usually in days, possibly in weeks or months.

tailoring: Duration estimates may include contingency reserve for risks from uncertainty in the estimates, ambiguity in the scope, or resource availability.
Estimate at the level of accuracy the project needs. Rolling wave planning is often used: as more is known about the activities, the estimates are refined and updated.
For projects using an agile development approach, set time boxes are used instead of duration estimates, and different estimating methods are used.
agile_or_adaptive: For agile projects, set time boxes are used rather than duration estimates, and different estimating methods apply (Tailoring Tips, PDF page 82, printed page 71).

decisions.notes: The worksheet form 2.17 carries the arithmetic for the three quantitative methods.

decisions.notes: The book's conversion for people-driven work is hours divided by 8 for days and by 40 for weeks (PDF page 81, printed page 70). It gives no other conversion.

citation: Book of Forms form 2.16, PDF pages 81 to 82 (printed pages 70 to 71); blank form PDF page 83 (printed page 72)
notes: The blank form prints Duration Estimate where Table 2.15 says Duration estimates; the printed label wins. The prose says estimates include at least ID, activity description and effort hours (PDF page 81, printed page 70), and the table adds the duration itself. The hours-to-days rule (divide by 8) and hours-to-weeks rule (divide by 40) are the book's, applied to durations driven by people rather than materials or equipment. The book's 'receives from' list names the resource breakdown structure twice; it is listed once here. The book spells the process 6.4 Estimate Activity Durations here and Estimate Activity Duration on form 2.17.
